units.description: Harvests gold/lumber, constructs buildings. Fights poorly.
Cheap melee line unit. Tanks for archers.
Long-range attacker. Fragile; keep behind footmen.

The Champion: melee hero, levels from nearby enemy deaths, AoE Slam ability. Your team's FIRST hero is FREE (the 25s and the 5 supply are still real, and both are spent at the hall that makes your workers); every hero after it — a second class, or this one back from the dead — costs revive_gold/revive_lumber, which is why that pair doubles as the fielding price. Revival preserves the level. Occupies one hero slot; slots scale with your hall tier (1/2/3) and no team may field two of the same class.
Siege engine: outranges towers, 6x damage vs buildings, but slow, fragile, and feeble against units. Escort it.
Fast cavalry: 2x damage vs Catapults, excels at worker raids and map control. Melts under massed fire.

Support hero: ranged attack, Heal ability (AoE ally healing). Free only if she is your team's first hero ever; standing alongside a Champion costs revive_gold/revive_lumber, the same price her death does — a Keep grants the SLOT, not the hero. Revival preserves the level. Occupies one hero slot.
Cheap anti-cavalry line: 5x damage vs Raiders and Knights, and the cheapest hit points in the game. Slow, and feeble against anything that isn't mounted.

Tier-2 caster (Arcane Sanctum, requires a Keep): auto-casts Slow, a -40% move and attack speed debuff on every enemy within 8 for 5s. Blunts cavalry charges and covers retreats. Barely fights; keep it behind the line.

Requires a Castle. Heavy shock cavalry: 350 hp at speed 9.5, no type bonus, just the best raw stats on the field. Breaks Footman and Archer lines at equal gold. Counter it with Spearmen — the Knight is cavalry, so it takes 5x from a spear, and 270g of Knight loses to 270g of Spearmen. Melee: cannot touch air.

Requires a Castle; trained at the Workshop. Flying: ignores walls, forests and chokepoints entirely, and attacks both ground and air. Melee units and Catapults CANNOT hit it at all — only Archers, the Priestess and Towers can. Counter it with massed Archers: 270g of Archers beats one Gryphon. Sees 26, the widest eye in the game.
Harvests gold/lumber, constructs buildings. Fights poorly.
Melee line unit: tankier than a Footman, slower, and slightly worse damage. Wins the duel, loses the chase.
Ranged line unit: harder hitting than an Archer and much shorter ranged. Thrown axes, so it answers air.

Requires a Fortress. Fast cavalry: 2x damage vs siege engines, excels at worker raids and map control. Cheaper and faster than a Raider, and dies quicker. Counter it with spears — it is cavalry, so a Spearman or an Impaler takes 5x off it.
Cheap anti-cavalry line: 5x damage vs any cavalry, of either race — Raiders, Knights and Wolfriders alike. Slow, and feeble against anything unmounted.
Requires a Fortress. Siege engine: outranges towers, 6x damage vs buildings, but slow, fragile, and feeble against units. Escort it.

Tier-2 caster (Spirit Lodge, requires a Fortress): auto-casts Bloodlust, thrown up to 8 away, giving every ally within 5 of it +20% damage and +25% move speed for 10s. Compounds a push; worthless in a retreat. Barely fights; keep it behind the line.

The Warchief: melee hero, levels from nearby enemy deaths, AoE Cleave ability. Your team's FIRST hero is FREE (the 25s and the 5 supply are still real, and both are spent at the hall that makes your workers); every hero after him — a second class, or this one back from the dead — costs revive_gold/revive_lumber, which is why that pair doubles as the fielding price. Revival preserves the level. Occupies one hero slot; slots scale with your hall tier (1/2/3) and no team may field two of the same class.

Support hero: ranged attack, Mend ability (AoE ally healing), and the widest eye of any ground unit in the game. Free only if he is your team's first hero ever; standing alongside a Warchief costs revive_gold/revive_lumber, the same price his death does — a Fortress grants the SLOT, not the hero. Revival preserves the level. Occupies one hero slot.

Requires a Hold; trained at the Spirit Lodge. Flying: ignores walls, forests and chokepoints entirely, and attacks both ground and air. Melee units and Demolishers CANNOT hit it at all — only Headhunters, Shamans, the FarSeer and Watchtowers can. Counter it with massed Headhunters. Sees 26, the widest eye in the game.

buildings.description: Tier 1 hall. Resource drop-off. Trains Workers and heroes (1 hero slot). Upgrades to a Keep.
Trains Footmen, Archers and Spearmen (Raiders once a Workshop stands, Knights once a Castle does).
+6 supply. Build ahead of the cap or production stalls.
Static defense: shoots arrows at enemies in range.
Cheap blocking segment. No function except HP in the way.
Siege works: trains Catapults, and Gryphon Riders once a Castle stands. Both answers to a tower turtle — one knocks the door down, the other flies over it.
Item vendor: heroes buy consumables here (see catalog items).

Tier 2 forge (requires a Keep). Researches the two team-wide ladders in catalog.research: Attack (+1/+2/+3 flat damage on every UNIT attack) and Armor (+1/+2/+3 flat damage reduction on every UNIT hit taken, never below 1 damage per hit). Bonuses are permanent, retroactive to units already alive, and survive the Blacksmith's death. One research at a time per forge; build a second Blacksmith to run both ladders at once.

Tier 2 hall: everything the TownHall was, with a deeper HP pool. Opens a SECOND hero slot (distinct classes only) and unlocks tier-2 content such as the Arcane Sanctum. Satisfies tier-1 requirements. Upgrades to a Castle.
Tier 3 hall: the top of the ladder. A third hero slot (unusable until a third hero class ships). Satisfies every hall requirement below it.
Arcane Sanctum: trains Sorcerers. Requires a Keep — the first thing a hall upgrade unlocks.
Tier 1 hall. Resource drop-off. Trains Peons and heroes (1 hero slot). Upgrades to a Fortress.
Trains Grunts, Headhunters and Impalers (Wolfriders and Demolishers once a Fortress stands). The Horde's entire ground army out of one building.
+6 supply, and stabs at ground enemies that come within 9. Feeble on purpose — it punishes an unescorted worker raid, it does not hold a line, and it cannot touch air.
Static defense: hurls spears at enemies in range, air included.
Spirit Lodge: trains Shamans, and Wyverns once a Hold stands. Requires a Fortress — the first thing a hall upgrade unlocks.

Tier 2 forge (requires a Fortress). Researches the same two team-wide ladders the Blacksmith does: Attack and Armor. Bonuses are permanent, retroactive to units already alive, and survive the WarMill's death. One research at a time per forge.

Tier 2 hall: everything the Stronghold was, with a deeper HP pool. Opens a SECOND hero slot (distinct classes only) and unlocks tier-2 content — the Spirit Lodge, the WarMill, Wolfriders and Demolishers. Satisfies tier-1 requirements. Upgrades to a Hold.
Tier 3 hall: the top of the Horde ladder, and the gate on the Wyvern. A third hero slot (unusable until a third Horde hero class ships). Satisfies every hall requirement below it.

research.name: Weapon Smithing
research.description: +1 damage per level on every attack made by one of your UNITS. Flat and applied last, so it is never multiplied by a Catapult's siege bonus or a hero's level. Does not arm Towers — research equips the army.

research.name: Armor Plating
research.description: -1 damage per level from every hit taken by one of your UNITS, floored at 1 damage per hit. Does not protect buildings — a Keep upgrade is what thickens masonry.

items.description: Instantly restores 150 HP to the hero.
Teleports the hero and nearby own units to one of your own standing halls. Destination is CHOOSABLE: use_item takes an optional `destination` building id; omit it for the hall nearest the hero.
Hastes the hero: +40% move speed for 15s.
Plants a banner: own units within 8 take 30% less damage for 10s.

Recalls the hero and EVERY own non-worker unit on the map to one of your own standing halls. Destination is CHOOSABLE: use_item takes an optional `destination` building id; omit it for the hall nearest the hero. Aiming it at the hall that is NOT nearest is the whole point — an army at the expansion defends the main by porting away from itself.

playbooks.label: Standard Kingdom
playbooks.pitch: Ten workers, a Barracks before three minutes, eyes on mid before four, a second mine before the first runs dry, and a tier bought only when there is something to spend it on.

steps.title: Ten workers before anything clever
steps.why: A worker costs 75 gold and has paid for itself in about ninety seconds, so an idle hall in the first three minutes is compound interest you never get back — and armed as a pulse this costs you nothing per cycle, where hand-queueing each Worker costs a whole poll you could have spent deciding something.

exits.title: Farm first — buy the supply the pulse is about to eat
exits.why: 80g/20l is the cheapest thing on the board, and a capped hall trains nothing at any price; if supply_used is within two of supply_cap this is the step and the pulse is not.

exits.title: Take the free hero now
exits.why: Your first hero is free and every one after it is 400g/100l, so the only bad time to take it is later — and it scouts, which is the one thing ten workers cannot do for you.

steps.title: A Barracks in the ground before the third minute
steps.why: r27's winner did not field a combat unit until t=165 and survived only because its mirror was exactly as slow; 160g/60l here is what buys you the ability to answer anything at all, and a plan with no answer in it is a plan that depends on your opponent's manners.

exits.title: Spearmen instead of Footmen — three bodies for the price of two
exits.why: 90g against 135g: when you are behind on bodies rather than on gold, count is the stat that stops a raid, and you can upgrade the composition later.

exits.title: Turtle first, build behind the line
exits.why: A Barracks going up in front of somebody already inside your base is 160 gold donated; hold the ring, then put it down thirty seconds later with the same worker.

steps.title: Stamp the doctrine once, and every new body inherits it
steps.why: A squad outlives its own members and an entity id does not, so stamping the Barracks once means every Footman it ever trains walks out already enrolled and already carrying squad 1's stance — the difference between one command now and one command per unit for the rest of the match.

exits.title: Enrol what is already standing
exits.why: The template only catches what the Barracks trains from here on; anything already alive is still loose and answers to nobody, which is how an army of six fights as six armies of one.

exits.title: Rally them somewhere useful while you mass
exits.why: New units walk to the rally point by themselves, so a gathered squad and a trickle differ by exactly one command that you send exactly once.

steps.title: Be standing at mid by the fourth minute
steps.why: Both r27 seats played a whole 791-second game without meaningful contact and each read the other's passivity as safety; a staged squad at mid is not an attack, it is the cheapest scout you own and the only way a number ever gets into your intel ledger before you need one.

exits.title: Harass instead of stage — their workers, not their army
exits.why: Harass breaks off at 55% and hunts workers first, so it spends your cheap units against their income rather than against their line, which is the trade you want while you are still the smaller army.

exits.title: Hold home and scout with the hero alone
exits.why: One hero at mid buys the same sighting for none of the squad, and if your army is the only thing between them and your hall then the sighting is all you can afford to pay for.

steps.title: Take the second mine while the first still has gold in it
steps.why: An expansion begun when the mine runs dry arrives about forty seconds after your income stopped, and both r28 seats' fatal errors were resource judgment of exactly that shape — 385g/205l is a price you pay comfortably now and cannot pay at all later, which is the whole argument.

exits.title: The other flank instead
exits.why: The two flank mines sit the same distance from both bases, so the only thing that separates them is which one they are standing on — take the other.

exits.title: Skip the expansion and buy the tier instead
exits.why: 320g/160l against 385g/205l: if your first mine is still fat, the Keep turns the same gold into units they cannot answer instead of into more gold you already have.

steps.title: Upgrade the hall — but only because of what comes after it
steps.why: r27's Sonnet put a naked Keep down at t=27 with zero army and never bought one tier-2 thing with it, which made 320 gold into a taller building; this upgrade is worth its price only as the first half of the step after it, so do not start it unless you mean to finish it.

exits.title: Workshop first — Raiders and Catapults are tier one
exits.why: 140g/100l unlocks Raiders at the Barracks you already own and Catapults for the buildings nothing else of yours can kill, and it never touches the hall.

exits.title: A second Barracks — one building cannot out-produce two
exits.why: If what you are losing is the unit count, then doubling the rate you make units is 160g/60l and beats any tier you could buy with the same gold.

steps.title: Buy something with tier 2 in the same minute you reach it
steps.why: A tier is a shopping list and not a score: 150g/130l of Sanctum turns into Sorcerers that arrive with Slow already on autocast and change how every fight after them resolves, whereas a Keep with nothing behind it is the 4,000-gold float the ladder watched Sonnet sit on for 35 cycles.

exits.title: Blacksmith, and buy the research
exits.why: Weapon Smithing is 100g/50l and applies to every unit you own and every unit you will ever own, which makes it the only purchase in the game that gets better the longer the match runs.

exits.title: Spend it on bodies, not buildings
exits.why: A tech building that finishes after the fight it was meant for is a building you paid to lose with; if they are already at your ford the answer is Footmen and it is Footmen right now.

steps.title: One squad, ten bodies, a healthy hero — then walk
steps.why: r26's red committed thirteen units into twelve defenders on an empty intel ledger, and r23's blue lost its push at four bodies and won the same push at eight; consolidation is the cheapest of the three push gates the document measures and the only one you can fix with a single command.

exits.title: Secure the expansion instead of massing for a push
exits.why: Secure holds a 30-radius ring around a mine, its workers and the approach, which is the thing a second base is actually worth defending with rather than a turtle ring around a hall nobody is attacking.

exits.title: Send what you have at their workers
exits.why: If you cannot win the fight then do not have it — harassment turns a squad too small to push into income they have to stop mining in order to answer.

steps.title: Commit, and commit all of it
steps.why: Push carries no leash and breaks off only at 25% because a squad that flinches at the enemy's ramp has spent the entire walk for nothing; the decision is made here, at arm time, and the one thing that must not happen after it is reinforcements arriving in ones.

exits.title: Break off to mid and re-form
exits.why: Stage pulls the survivors into a 10-radius ring and holds them there, which is how a push that went badly becomes an army again instead of a casualty list.

exits.title: Full recall — your base is worth more than the trade
exits.why: Turtle anchors on your own hall and breaks off at 45%; if their counter-attack is already inside your base then the push is no longer the most expensive thing on the board.

steps.title: If it goes long, tier 3 is what breaks the stalemate
steps.why: Every round of the ladder ended before anybody reached tier 3, so a fifteen-minute game is one nobody in this arena has yet played well: Knights are 270g/60l of cavalry that no tier-1 composition answers, and 480g/240l for the Castle is affordable exactly once a second mine has been running for five minutes.

exits.title: Gryphons instead — nothing they own shoots up
exits.why: 280g/120l of Air, and an opponent with no answer to it has to rebuild their whole composition from scratch while you keep flying over the one they had.

exits.title: A third base rather than a third tier
exits.why: A Castle you can only afford once is worse than two mines you can afford twice; if the thing that is behind is your income, then fix your income.
